seoTitle: Zanzibar (Mjini Magharibi) Travel Guide 2026 — Beaches, Culture & Tours
intro: Mjini Magharibi — Zanzibar's urban west region — contains Stone Town, the island's ancient capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with some of the Indian Ocean's most beautiful beaches. Zanzibar Archipelago sits 35 kilometres off Tanzania's coast, shaped by centuries of Arab, Persian, Indian, and Portuguese trade that left behind a layered culture unlike anywhere else in East Africa. The island's spice farms, historic slave market, pristine reefs, and turquoise lagoons make it one of Africa's most complete destinations.

sections.heading: Stone Town — The Old City
sections.content: Stone Town is Zanzibar's medieval heart, a UNESCO-listed warren of coral-stone alleys, carved hardwood doors, Persian-influenced mosques, and colonial-era buildings. The Old Fort (Ngome Kongwe), built by the Omani Arabs in the 17th century, hosts evening cultural performances. The House of Wonders, once the largest building in East Africa, is being restored after partial collapse. The former slave market and Anglican Cathedral stand as a sobering memorial to the island's 19th-century role as the Indian Ocean's largest slave trading port. Forodhani Gardens come alive at sunset with street food vendors selling Zanzibar mix, fresh seafood, and sugarcane juice. Budget a full day minimum for Stone Town.

sections.heading: Beaches of West Zanzibar
sections.content: The west coast around Stone Town has calm, clear water sheltered from the Indian Ocean swell. Kendwa Beach (north) is Zanzibar's most social beach — the weekly full-moon party draws travellers from across the island. Nungwi, at the northern tip, sits above the tidal line so swimming is possible at any hour regardless of tide. The east coast (Paje, Bwejuu) has stronger winds ideal for kite-surfing but dramatic tidal flats that strand visitors at low tide. For the clearest snorkelling water, Mnemba Atoll — a 30-minute boat ride offshore — is one of the best dive sites in the western Indian Ocean.

sections.heading: Spice Farm Tours
sections.content: Zanzibar was the world's dominant clove producer for most of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The island still grows cloves, cinnamon, vanilla, nutmeg, black pepper, turmeric, lemongrass, and cardamom on working farms in the central interior. Half-day spice tours from Stone Town visit active farms where guides identify plants by smell and taste, explain traditional uses, and prepare a Swahili lunch. Tours cost $25–40 per person including transport. Booking through a verified operator on GetYourGuide ensures a licensed guide and avoids the unofficial touts who inflate prices mid-tour.

sections.heading: Prison Island and Marine Life
sections.content: Changuu Island — nicknamed Prison Island — sits 20 minutes by speedboat from Stone Town. A British detention facility built in 1893 and never used for prisoners, it now houses a sanctuary for Aldabra giant tortoises, some over 100 years old. The surrounding reef offers excellent shallow snorkelling in 3–8 metres of water. Dolphins are resident year-round at Kizimkazi on the southwest coast — morning boat tours allow snorkelling alongside Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins. Whale sharks visit Zanzibar's offshore waters between October and March; specialist dive operators run dedicated whale shark experiences.

sections.heading: Getting to and Around Zanzibar
sections.content: Fast ferries from Dar es Salaam run several times daily — the crossing takes 75–90 minutes and costs $35–45 for tourists. Book in advance; morning services sell out. Flights from Dar es Salaam are 20 minutes on small turboprops — expensive ($120–200) but worth it if time is short. Within Zanzibar, dalla-dallas (shared minibuses) connect Stone Town to most beach villages for $0.50–2. Private transfers to Nungwi cost $30–35 one way. Renting a scooter ($20/day) is the most flexible option for exploring the island's interior spice farms and villages.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Zanzibar?
faqs.a: June to October is peak season — minimal rainfall, calm seas, ideal for beaches and diving. January to February is also excellent: dry, slightly quieter, and cheaper than peak. Avoid April–May (long rains) and November (short rains) if you want reliable beach weather. Water temperature stays around 26°C year-round.

Yes. Zanzibar is one of East Africa's safest tourist destinations. The island has a well-developed tourism infrastructure and is accustomed to international visitors. Standard precautions apply: don't walk alone in isolated areas at night, keep valuables secured, and use licensed transport. Dress modestly in Stone Town as it is a predominantly Muslim community.

faqs.q: How do I get from Zanzibar to mainland Tanzania?
faqs.a: Fast ferries to Dar es Salaam run daily, taking 75–90 minutes ($35–45). Flights are 20 minutes to Dar or 30 minutes to Kilimanjaro Airport. For a Kilimanjaro climb itinerary, fly Zanzibar to JRO directly rather than going through Dar.

faqs.q: Do I need a visa for Zanzibar separately?
faqs.a: No. Zanzibar is part of Tanzania — your standard Tanzanian tourist visa ($50, available on arrival or e-visa) covers both the mainland and Zanzibar. East African Community nationals enter without a visa.

faqs.q: What currency is used in Zanzibar?
faqs.a: Tanzanian Shillings (TZS) are the official currency. USD is widely accepted at tourist establishments. ATMs in Stone Town accept international cards but can be unreliable — bring some USD cash. Most tours and accommodation quote in USD.

tips: Dress modestly in Stone Town — cover shoulders and knees out of respect for the local Muslim community
Check tide times before swimming on the east coast — low tide exposes 500m of sand flats
Book the Forodhani night market street food early evening before the best dishes run out
The best snorkelling at Mnemba Atoll requires calm weather — avoid going after overnight rain
Negotiate dhow tours the evening before, not morning of — prices spike at departure time
Carry small USD bills or local currency for markets and dalla-dallas
